utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. So this is Tuesday, and I welcome the OTP, the representative of the OTP, as well as the witness, Mr. Seselj, and everyone helping us. We're in Courtroom II today. Normally, we're in Courtroom I or III, but these courtrooms were unavailable, notably Courtroom III, which is why we were sent to Courtroom II. However, this will only be temporary. Today, we shall be hearing the witness in the courtroom today. But before this, I would like to move to private session quickly. But before this, Mr. Seselj, on an administrative matter, I believe you had something to say. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have three administrative issues to raise, but they'll be brief. I have to inform you, firstly, that the Prosecution, along with this registrar of documents which it intends to use during the examination of this witness, once again provided me with a list exclusively in English, and it's a ten-page documents. I think you must instruct the Prosecution never to repeat that again and to issue instructions that I be provided with a copy in Serbian forthwith. There are a number of descriptions here of various documents, and you can see that it is a long document. That's the first point. Secondly, over the weekend I looked through the documents to do with the coming witness, VS-051, who is scheduled to appear next week, and I found that I was lacking certain materials from his transcript, the transcript of his testimony and another trial. The Prosecutor knows full well what the trial is. I don't want to mention the name of the trial, not to disclose the witness's identity, but anyway and I need his testimony on the 16th of February and perhaps earlier on if it began on the 15th too, as well as his testimony of the 22nd of February from 1805 hours in the afternoon, and if it went on to the next day. I was provided by them by about 240 pages of transcript, and reading through it, I found out that I was missing some parts. So I demand that I be supplied with that as soon as possible, because without it, I won't be able to cross-examine the witness next week. So they have to provide me with that by Friday. And the third point is this: To avoid writing a written submission, I don't want to burden you, 15 minutes before I entered court the representative of the Registrar provided me with a public document. It was the request by the Stanisic Defence for access to confidential testimony and exhibits in the Seselj rule [as interpreted] on the basis of Rule 75 (G) and (I). Now, as I am expected to present my views and to speed up the whole process and not have to write a written submission, I telling you now, here and now that I agree that the Stanisic Defence be given access to all confidential testimony and documents in the trial against me, and I consider that it is enough for this to be on the record of today's proceedings, that I don't need to submit this in writing as well. So that's all I had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let's take them -- let's take these three points in the reverse order. We'll start with the last one, the Stanisic submission. We have taken due note of your agreement, and the Trial Chamber will make a decision very quickly on this. Now, to the second point, for Witness VS-051, obviously you're missing a few documents, so I would like the Prosecution to check this. Yes, Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Simply to say, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'll certainly look into the matter. I believe that we have attempted to make all the disclosures that we have available, but I will not be leading that witness, and so I will confer with the attorney who will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding the document written in English, according to Mr. Seselj, I don't know which document it is. It seems to be -- could you help us? Which document is it, Mrs. Biersay, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe the document to which Mr. Seselj is referring is the index to the court binder that gives a general description of the 65 ter numbers of the documents in the binder, as well as the description and ERN numbers. Certainly, I think given the fast turnaround that we had with the binder, we didn't have the resources to direct to provide that index in English -- in B/C/S, and so we had to make a judgement call in getting it to Mr. Seselj as soon as possible of delaying it in order to provide the index in B/C/S, and the decision was made to get it to him as soon as we could in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please, in the future, try to ensure that Mr. Seselj obtains this document, this index, in his own language. It's not very complicated, obviously, to translate. The there are a number of photographs. Photographs in Serbian is probably very simple to translate. There are two transcripts of phone conversations, obviously. It should only take a few minutes to translate. Very well. Let me now ask for a private session for a few minutes. Mr. Seselj first, you wanted to add something or to respond to Mrs. Biersay maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small correction with respect to Witness VS-051. I'm expecting to be disclosed in all the documents. I assume that they'll be doing that by Friday. But I'm talking about the transcript of the testimony of that particular witness in another trial, in other proceedings. And since he's only testified in one other trial, then the Prosecutor knows which trial it was. I don't have to mention the name of the trial. So the transcript is not complete. The first part and last part are missing, and in fact I specified, when I first took the floor, what was missing, what portions were missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move to private session, but for another topic. Mrs. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Biersay, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you tell the members of the Trial Chamber where you were born and where you were raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was born in Belgrade, and I was raised in Belgrade, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What level of education did you complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed the secondary architectural school, and then I went to the machine engineering school; and I was trained as a building construction technician and tinsmith. And I became employed with the JNA as a civilian. And I -- in our country, there was what was called "streamed education" that was ongoing. That was the system. So the secondary school of architecture, there were a number of branches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make. The microphone doesn't seem to be working, the witness's microphone, and I can't hear him properly. My microphone is in order. It's the witness's that isn't working properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, for how long did you work as a civilian with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About four years and a few months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to direct your attention to the period of time when the JNA started mobilising reservists to Croatia in 1991. At some point, Mr. Witness, did you decide to become a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I decided to become a volunteer in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for which organisation did you decide to join as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I decided to join the Serbian Chetnik movement or, rather, the Serbian Radical Party, Vojislav Seselj's party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why did you decide to join that party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because my family nurtures monarchist traditions, so that seemed to me to be most suitable. As far as I'm concerned, I didn't like communism so it suited me, and at that time it was propagated that the Chetnik Party -- well, that particular party. I didn't know at the time they were not actually for the monarchy, but I wasn't politically literate at the time so I didn't really know all these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you were joining this party because you thought it represented your monarchist ideas?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. That question is absolutely impermissible. The Prosecutor is asking whether it is true and correct that you joined the party because you believed that it represented monarchist ideals and ideas. The Prosecutor must not put questions like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I don't understand your objection. Mrs. Biersay is asking the witness why he joined the Serbian Chetnik Party. She's asking for the reasons behind this. This is at line 14 -- page 14, line 9. And he answers: "Because my family had a monarchist tradition," which is interesting. When we'd like to know why someone decides to volunteer and joins the Chetnik Party. And that's the reason. It's useful to know why this person volunteered, so I'll ask the question, a follow-up question. Witness, please, according to what you said, it seems that you volunteered because your family was monarchist. It means obviously your family wanted to have a king to lead Serbia. Was this the whole idea behind your joining?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's right. My family, before the war, before World War II, that is, were always in favour of the king.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you joined this political party or this movement, this political movement, did you have any friends who had the same ideas and who joined the movement also because they were monarchists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in -- well, in 99 per cent of the volunteers, had the same ideas I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 99 per cent of the volunteers who joined the Chetnik movement were monarchists; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Almost saying 100 per cent, actually. Very well. Mrs. Biersay, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you go in order to join the Serbian Chetnik movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the Serbian Radical Party, which was on Ohridska Street, because I had information that that's where one could join the volunteers. The media advertised this. They said, "You should go through Seselj," and that the Chetniks were going to the front to assist the people on the battlefield. So I joined them, that's where I went. I asked around, asked my friends, and they said "That's the place -- that's the best place to go, that's the best place for you, because all the Chetniks are there."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Approximately when did you go to this office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in 1991, I think in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you went to the office, who did you meet there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went to the office, I was received there by Zoran Rankic. He was the deputy chief of the War Staff there, and he was wearing a military uniform, all spick and span. I thought he was some sort of general, but later on I came to realise that he wasn't. And he received me, he wrote my name down, and said that I was automatically a member of the Serbian Radical Party, having come as a volunteer, to apply as a volunteer. I was interested in other matters, and I asked him how I was going to justify the fact that I was off work, and he said, "There's no problem there. We're going to issue you with a certificate, so that will settle that as far as your job is concerned." And he said -- well, he wrote my name in as a member, and he said he'd call me up on the phone when enough volunteers had rallied together to go to Western Slavonia, that he would inform me when that would be, where, what day and what time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let's discuss that certificate, that document that Mr. Rankic mentioned to you that would help you with your job. What exactly was that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a certificate which Ljubisa Petkovic usually wrote out if the volunteers needed it. We would go to ask for a certificate to let us off work, to justify our absence from work. And, for example, the volunteers didn't have to pay for their electricity. You would take your certificate saying you're a volunteer to the electrical distribution network and you wouldn't have to pay. And when you would have certificates like that, too, when you did your military service of any kind, they would write this down in your military booklet and then this would give you extra years of service. Every year you served would be counted as two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What other types of professions received that double counting of military service that you just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the army, the JNA, and the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just so that I'm clear, people in the police and in the army would receive credit for double the time that they actually served in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if you were an SRS volunteer, a Serbian Chetnik Movement volunteer, you would also get the same benefit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The question is complicated, Witness. This is the first time that we've been hearing about this, which is why I'm quite interested by it. We have just been told that a volunteer did not pay his electricity bill, and secondly, that all the time spent in the army was going to count double, probably for his pension and retirement. This is what you just said; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, those are my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Now, these benefits, which are quite important, according to you, were they granted because you were a volunteer or because you were a member of the Chetnik movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the benefits and credits were authorised by the top people in the state, because Vojislav Seselj collaborated very closely with the top authorities in the states, so we enjoyed all the benefits that the officers in the army benefitted from. And this was decided at the very top leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying it was the state that granted these benefits, but you're drawing the conclusion that it is because Mr. Seselj was collaborating with state authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. In the Serbian armies, these volunteers, were they people who were under the law, in general? They were under the law, but I would like to know one thing. I'd like to know whether all the other volunteers were granted the same benefits or only the volunteers who were organised by the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, it was only the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party that enjoyed those benefits. However, other volunteers most probably did, too, because this was regulated by law. That's 100 per cent correct. And I'm sure they enjoyed those benefits and credits too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was a problem with translation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... or that they could enjoy those rights, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe there's a little problem with translation, because it seems that there's a contradiction in your answer. You were saying earlier that only the volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party were granted these benefits, and then later on you're saying that maybe the other volunteers too, so could you be more specific, as far as you're concerned, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I added and said that other volunteers probably didn't have the proper information telling them that they could avail themselves of those benefits. They didn't know about it. We did have information from the chief of the War Staff, Ljubisa Petkovic, that we were entitled to those benefits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we understood you well, as far as you're concerned, you are telling us that this possibility of being granted benefits was told to you, which is why you took advantage of it, as well as all your other friends from the Serbian Radical Party. But you're saying for other volunteers coming from other parties, if they hadn't gotten the information, they might not have benefitted from all this? Is this what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I understood. Thank you. Mrs. Biersay, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, these certificates that you're discussing, where they issued by the SRS or were they issued by another state organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those certificates were issued by the War Staff of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to the benefits that you just described, did you have any discussions with anyone at the SRS, the Serbian Chetnik Movement, about health insurance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did talk to Zoran Rankic and Ljubisa Petkovic. I did discuss that, so that could be regulated as well. In principle, if the volunteer needed anything, they would go to the War Staff and be issued a certificate, and this would usually be issued by Ljubisa Petkovic. They would be issued a certificate for whatever he needed, whether for his electricity bills, or his work post, the employment bureau, or whatever, for his social insurance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: During your discussion, when you went to register with the SRS, during your discussion with Mr. Rankic, did he describe what role Mr. Seselj played in the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he was the chief there, that he was the main boss, that he was the supreme commander. And he introduced himself to me as the deputy of the War Staff, and he said that he was there to register the volunteers who applied and to inform them about their departure for the front, for the frontline, the war theatre. And he said that the party would take all necessary measures to protect its volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was your understanding about the relationship between the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood it to be a serious organisation, which is why I applied. I thought that in time, as the JNA was down on its knees, the Serbian Chetnik Movement would take over control in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did anyone explain to you in what way the Serbian Chetnik Movement was connected to the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, no one did. I wasn't informed as to the manner in which it was connected. Later on, I came to understand that it was one section. It was rumoured among the people that they couldn't register the Serbian Chetnik Movement, so they registered the Serbian Radical Party instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why were they -- why could they not register the Serbian Chetnik Movement, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that, but that's what people said to attract people, to get them to come in and volunteer, in fact to misuse them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you registered as a volunteer at the SRS office in Belgrade, did you in fact get a call from Mr. Rankic later about deployment to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After about a month or two, Rankic called me up, and he said that there would be buses leaving. They were parked in the 27th of March Street and that they would be leaving at 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning. I'm not sure about the time anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How much time passed between the time he called you and the time these buses were supposed to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about four or five days, more or less. I can't be precise about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where -- what was your understanding about where you were going to be deployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had already been told that we were going to Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe the circumstances when you went to the area to which Mr. Rankic had directed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We set out in the buses --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could stop you for one minute, Mr. Witness. Could you describe for the Trial Chamber the situation where the buses were? At what address did you go to meet the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the 27 Marta, the 27th of March Street in Belgrade, near the botanical gardens. There was a clearing where the buses stood. We were sitting in a restaurant across the road, waiting for Rankic and the commander that the Serbian Radical Party had designated to come along. Some of the volunteers were already drunk. When Radovan Novacic came, Rankic told us he was our commander. We boarded the buses. Radovan Novacic didn't want to take those who were drunk, he didn't want to take them with him, and there was a small conflict with Zoran Rankic because Rankic wanted to take them, but Radovan Novacic said, "Either those who are drunk will leave or I will leave," so that those who were drunk did not go. But we did go, and Radovan went with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if I could stop you for one minute. How many volunteers ended up boarding the buses to leave to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 27 in all. I can't say whether there were 25 or 27, but the first group was rather small. I mean, the bus wasn't full.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did Mr. Rankic go on the buses with the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he went back to the War Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to rejecting volunteers because they were drunk, did Mr. Novacic reject volunteers based on what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen. The ones who were drunk said they were going there to kill, to slaughter, to gouge people's eyes out, and that's why he didn't want to take them. And when we got on the buses, he said, "If anyone is going there in order to slaughter people, he can leave right now."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of Mr. Novacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is half Croat, half Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The number of volunteers that you described for the Trial Chamber, were they all SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all volunteers who had reported to the Serbian Radical Party and applied to go to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what route the bus took to get to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We couldn't go through Croatia, so we went through Bosnia. We spent the night in Bosanska Gradiska. There was a prison there and the JNA barracks --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Witness. Before we discuss where you stopped, I just wanted generally for you to describe the route that you took to get to Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, there were lots of people check-points, since there was a state of war, so we went through Bosnian territory because that area had not yet been affected by the war. We went via Doboj. The police greeted us along the way because they had been informed we would be coming through, so that we didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could see 65 ter number 7187, please. And while we're calling it up, 65 ter number 7187 is a map with the northern-marked area being Vocin, to the south Banja Luka, and Sid to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, where was the first stop that you made on your way to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our first stop was Bosanska Gradiska. We stayed in the prison there, and there was a JNA barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you got to Bosanska Gradiska, did anyone from that area greet the bus of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Goran Hadzic was there, so was Dzakula, and some other representatives of the government of Western Slovenia. They greeted us and they put us in the barracks to stay with the army. The army had taken refuge there temporarily because it was a war area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the barracks in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one night, we just spent one night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the following days, the army from Vocin arrived by bus. They came from Western Slavonia with a driver in a camouflage uniform, and they took us to Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This driver, was he armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two of them, in fact, in camouflage uniforms. The driver was armed with a pistol, and the other driver, also wearing a camouflage uniform, was also armed. He had an automatic rifle. They followed us, Hadzic and Dzakula, I mean. Dzakula was the president of the municipality at the time. They followed us in a car: We, the volunteers, were taken there by bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The bus that you boarded in Bosanska Gradiska, was that the same bus that you had boarded in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was another bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And from Bosanska Gradiska, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you go next, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived in Vocin. There, we had lunch. And later on, they took us to a place called "Lager", where there was a reconnaissance sector overlooking Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that area referred to as the Papuk area or is it referred to by something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is the area of Mount Papuk. That's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when -- if someone referred to the area of Podravska Slatina, what area would they be talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a broader area, Podravska Slatina. It's lower down. That's Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp that you just described, were you given any weapons or uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived in the camp at around 5.00, and at about 9.00 in the evening the army brought weapons and uniforms by truck. These were old uniforms with the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you feel about wearing uniforms with the five-pointed star?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't wear civilian clothes, so I had to put it on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were the uniforms with the five-pointed star, were they camouflaged or non-camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were olive grey, drab, these ordinary old uniforms, and they were not intended for fighting, but for parades, because you couldn't even crouch down in them properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe to the Trial Chamber what type of weapons you were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were given new weapons. They were in crates which had not been unpacked. And they also brought us a barrel of oil so that we could take the grease off the weapons, so that we stayed up late into the night cleaning the weapons. And we also showed each other how to use the weapons, because many volunteers didn't know how to put the weapons together. So that Radovan had the first part of the training with the group about using the weapons, putting them together and taking them apart again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "Radovan," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to Radovan Novacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd now like to discuss with you the command structure for the area in which you were in Western Slavonia. Could you describe for the Trial Chamber the command that Radovan Novacic had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radovan Novacic was subordinate to Jovan Trbojevic, who was a lieutenant colonel of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. He could not make a decisions, unless it was an emergency, without Jovan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did Radovan Novacic have a title?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was a reserve captain, but he was the commander of the Serbian volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was he the commander of all the SRS volunteers in the Papuk area or only part of the Papuk area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first authorisation he got was to command all the volunteers in all of Western Slavonia, not just the Papuk area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you said that he was subordinated to Lieutenant Colonel Jovan Trbojevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who else was subordinated to Lieutenant Colonel Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police was also subordinated, as were the special units led by Zoran Miscevic. Let me explain. In wartime, everyone is subordinated to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. Witness. Who is Slavko Misic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who is Slavko Misic? I apologise for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavko Misic was later sent to the Okucani area, which is also in Western Slavonia, and he was issued with a certificate saying that he was a commander in the area. So there was a conflict between him and Radovan. He was also a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was Misic subordinated to someone else in that area, and if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was subordinated to Narandzic, who was an active-duty military person in that area. I can't recall his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is Zoran Miscevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in charge of the special units of the Army of Yugoslavia, and he was subordinated to Jovan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you described the first -- you described the number of volunteers who were on that bus with you. Did you have an impression about whether or not your bus was the first bus of volunteers in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were the first volunteers in that area. We were the first group.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you described that there were over 20 volunteers -- SRS volunteers on that trip. Did the number of SRS volunteers in that area change over time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The groups arrived, one after another. Of as soon as they had a full bus, they would inform Radovan, and we would go to meet those volunteers and bring them to the war theatre, so that there were quite a lot of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many volunteers would you estimate were there at the peak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about 400, I would say, at the peak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, of these 400 volunteers that you mentioned, were they all organised by the Serbian Radical Party or were they volunteers from elsewhere, organised by other associations, organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of what organisation they belonged to, they all came through the Radical Party, but in the end a bus of JNA reservists arrived at Zvecevo, where Trbojevic was, and that was a group of about 50 reservists who came towards the end; and they did not come through the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we'd move for the admission of the map which is 65 ter number 7187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar please give a number to this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be P312, Your Honours, marked for identification. Correction, Your Honours. This would be Exhibit P312.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I'd request that we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like you to explain to us if the volunteers, who presumably had no military experience or training, were offered training while they were staying at the camp in Vocin. I'm speaking about military training, that is to say, discipline, battle manoeuvring, and issues like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they did undergo military training. At the beginning, you couldn't have a volunteer there who didn't respect discipline, and the first group was trained personally by Radovan Novacic. Now, later on, they were trained by other volunteers, too, who went through their primary military course training well and got good marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this answer, without dealing in details, I would like to know one thing: Had you done your national service with the JNA; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did my military service in two parts, the JNA military service, but I didn't complete it; just the training bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, you had had some kind of military training. Your other colleagues, who were also volunteers, had they also done their military service with the JNA? You were volunteers, but all of you were at least over 21?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were volunteers who hadn't done their military service at all. The criminals came, too, and people came -- volunteers came in from various parts and walks of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you're introducing something new. You're saying that there were criminals. So in saying this, did you mean that these were people who had been convicted in court and who had then volunteered? Is this what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So these people who had been sentenced hadn't been -- hadn't done their military service within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, but there were other people, too that didn't do their military service, but were not convicted of anything, and that's why Radovan Novacic emphasised the fact that training was important, because most of them didn't know how to handle weapons, so as to avoid inflicting wounds upon oneself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Delinquents who joined as volunteers, I'd like to know, Novacic found this in Vocin, and this is when he found out there were these delinquents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would discover that in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Why is it that he didn't send them home at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases, he did send them back. If they didn't want to listen and lacked discipline, he would mostly send them back in most cases, and then he would complain to the War Staff about having sent all the riffraff to him and not having made a selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when Novacic found out that someone had a criminal record, was an offender, he would send him back right away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he would send them back straight away. If they refused to listen to discipline, because there were people who were ready to listen to discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the offenders who obeyed were kept. You were twice with the JNA, so when you were in Vocin, was the discipline in Vocin identical to the discipline within the JNA or was it more relaxed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The discipline, not in Vocin but in Lager, was stronger than in the JNA, and that's why Jovan Trbojevic said to Radovan Novacic on one occasion that he was happy to see him there because his men began behaving in a more disciplined fashion up to his arrival, and we set the example in terms of discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, as a conclusion, you seem to be saying that the volunteer's who were with you in that camp were even more disciplined than if they'd been in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you just described that Novacic would complain to the War Staff about the riffraff that they were sending him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the War Staff kept on sending riffraff, despite his complaints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did keep sending all sorts of people, despite his complaints.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to move back to the topic of the relationship between the SRS volunteers, through Novacic, and the TO and JNA. You mentioned that Novacic was in contact with the TO and JNA. Could you describe how he maintained that contact with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We maintained contact through radio link, and we received that from the JNA, or he would go directly to the headquarters to see Jovan Trbojevic in Zvecevo to discuss some matters that needed to be discussed regarding certain actions or weapons or things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How was coordination done in the field for military actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plans were made by Jovan Trbojevic. Radovan would be there to discuss the plans with him. But what do you actually mean? Did you mean -- well, we used Motorolas for communication purposes and radio links. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If volunteers were to be sent out into the field for military action, how would they know where to go and what to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they would receive orders by radio communication. They would tell us where we needed to go and what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is "they"? You say "they would tell us."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army would report to the War Staff in Lager, and the Lager would convey it to Radovan, and he would tell the volunteers where to go, pass the information on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any situations where Novacic would take the initiative as far as directing the SRS volunteers about where they should go or what they should do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As there were few of us at the beginning, he would make intervention platoons in order to be able to assist all the locals and the population generally in Western Slavonia in different areas, so that when he would receive information that something was happening somewhere, that's what he could do, but only in extreme situations; for example, when the volunteers hit an ambush, JNA, then the intervention platoon would go and pull them out. Then he would take the initiative. He wouldn't wait for orders from Jovan Trbojevic or authorisation from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who provided the food for the SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army did, the army provided food.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who provided fuel for the needs of the SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, the army, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who paid the salaries of the SRS volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army, the JNA again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With respect to salaries, were those salaries paid in the field or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was in the field, but later on it was paid out at the 4th of July barracks in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the questions of the Prosecutor lead me to asking another question which might make things clearer. You have just told us that the volunteers were dressed by the JNA, armed by the JNA, that they executed the orders of the JNA, that they were paid by the JNA. So according to you, what is the difference, on the field, between a JNA soldier and a soldier belonging to your unit? Is there a difference between the two or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a difference, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In ideology, ideology. We thought differently than -- to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What were you thinking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were in favour of the king and the homeland, and they were communists. And we used them, thinking that once we returned to Serbia, we would take over command over the JNA, because already at that time it was on its knees, it was completely degraded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, because I believe that this is very important, you were saying that the difference between you and the JNA is that they were communist, whereas you were monarchists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I understood you right, your objective was, and I'm using your words, because the JNA was on its knees, you were going to be able, through this, to take power; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But taking power, for you did that mean to set up a king?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And all your friends had the same feeling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you described for the Trial Chamber Novacic contacting the SRS War Staff in Belgrade to complain about the quality of the volunteers they were sending. Could you describe for us what kinds of contacts Novacic had with the SRS or Staff in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, usually he would have telephone communication to tell him who to contact from the war staff, various needs and requirements, or when he went to Belgrade he would report personally to Seselj in his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let's talk first about those telephone contacts. How often would Novacic contact the SRS War Staff in Belgrade by phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually, every two or three days, he would call up from Banja Luka or Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why did he call from those two places and not from where you were based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the telephone lines weren't working at the time in Western Slavonia, they weren't operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any SRS offices in the two places that you just described, either Banja Luka or Bosanska Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, offices did exist, and we would call from the Red Cross, too, from their offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where was the SRS office from which you would call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosanska Gradiska, that's where the office was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What type of information would Novacic convey to the SRS War Staff in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, usually he would recount what was happening on the ground and what was the problems were on the ground, so that they could help him solve the problems. At the beginning, there were problems with uniforms. We asked for more uniforms and additional weapons, because the number of volunteers had increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was your -- what was your perception of Novacic's duty to call the SRS War Staff? Was it something he chose to do or something that he had to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understood, it was something he had to do, because he had a superior above him, the War Staff. He was just the commander to whom the War Staff would issue instructions for him to be a commander, so he had to table reports to the War Staff, because in hierarchal terms they were above him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move into another segment. I'm not sure if the Court would like to take the break now or if I should just begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost time for the break, almost 10.30, so we will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we shall resume the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, before the break we were discussing the contacts that Novacic had with the SRS War Staff in Belgrade, and you described some telephonic contacts. When Novacic would call the SRS War Staff in Belgrade, do you know with whom he would speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would speak either to Vojislav Seselj or to Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did Novacic also have face-to-face meetings at the SRS War Staff in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the exception of Ljubisa Petkovic and Vojislav Seselj, he didn't have meetings with anyone, to the best of my knowledge in the War Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something I don't understand, and perhaps you can enlighten us. You explained to us that the JNA clothed volunteers, provided weapons, et cetera. Why was there a need to go via the Serbian Radical Party, and why telephone directly to this general, whereas the military chain of command was such that this type of problem could be solved? That's what I don't understand. Perhaps you can explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, they gave us weapons because there weren't many of us and they were able to arm us. Later on, the number of volunteers grew and there were a lot of us. The army at Zvecevo did not have enough weapons for all of us, so that we had to try and get weapons from Belgrade, from Serbia, for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said to us that Novacic depended on the colonel in the JNA, Trbojevic. Sorry about my pronunciation. Why was it not this colonel from the JNA who called the general to solve this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite honestly, I don't know. I assume that Trbojevic was a bad officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point when you were in Western Slavonia, did Mr. Seselj come to visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did he address the volunteers who were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did address the volunteers, yes, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was at Lager.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe the circumstances around his arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't expect him to come, but we were told that he was on his way, and Radovan Novacic told everybody to get ready, there were about 50 of us there, to get ready for the visit because Seselj would be coming, but not everybody managed to come out. He briefly said two sentences, got into his car, and left for Zvecevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did the volunteers feel about that brief meeting or address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were happy to see him, but most of them were disappointed because it was such a brief visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall what Mr. Seselj told those volunteers who were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was roughly this: "Kill all the enemy, but do not loot," something along those lines. I can't remember his exact words, but that was the meaning of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were all 50 -- the 50 volunteers that you just mentioned, were they all present for this brief address from Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not all of them were present. Some hadn't managed to get ready for the visit. They were still in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So how many volunteers were actually present for that address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj said, "Don't loot." Had there been looting by volunteers before his arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not by the volunteers, there were no instances of looting. But according to what we knew, everything had been looted when we arrived by the locals and the army, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Based on your interactions with the volunteers, could you describe how they viewed Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they viewed him -- most of them viewed him -- looked up to him as if he were a god.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because they considered him to be the person who would bring the king back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as you know, when -- well, Mr. Seselj, when he is said to have said that you had to kill all the enemy, as you said before, did that mean that they had to be killed during battle, in military terms, or was there a broader meaning within this phrase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how the others understood this, but I understood it as meaning that the Ustasha forces, the Croatian forces, were those who were supposed to be killed. I don't know how other people understood this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian forces who were in combat or also all Croats in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally understood it that it meant the Croatian forces where the fighting was going on. I don't know how other people understood it. I suppose every man understood it in his own way. All I can say is to speak for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go back to the sentence that Mr. Seselj allegedly said in front of the volunteers. What was the meaning of this sentence, according to you? Did it mean "kill them in combat, during the fight," according to rules of war, or did it have a broader sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood it that they should be killed in combat. I don't know how other volunteers understood this. That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in wartime, discipline is paramount. If discipline is observed, then military rules and laws can be obeyed. But if there's no discipline, then nothing is respected or obeyed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that information did arrive, and on television they showed how the population of Western Slavonia were fleeing the area on tractors, small vans, trucks and so on. And the reports said that there was general chaos in the region, and they did have information that some very strange things were going on over there. I personally didn't know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a minute. Let's take that bit by bit. You say that you saw on television that the population was leaving Western Slavonia. What population, the Serb population or the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian population was leaving the territory of Western Slavonia, and it was on the news, on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could see 65 ter number 4153. And I'll also give you the numbers for the others that will follow. I will ask for 4170, 4177, 4191, and 4221. And for the Court's information, these are photo stills taken from video 40000278, which has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, directing your attention to 65 ter number 4153, do you see anyone that you recognise in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Zoran Drazilovic, nicknamed "Cica" on the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, is he wearing on his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's wearing the "sajkaca" or peasant-style cap with a cockade on the cap and also on his lapel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it possible to have the witness mark with an "X" the person he has identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 4153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could now go to 65 ter number 4170, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, a technical question, before moving on. This person that we saw that had two cockades, one on his head or hat or beret and the other one on his jacket, what exactly does this cockade mean ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cockade designates the Serbian Chetnik Movement. All Chetniks wore these cockades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yourself, did you wear one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally didn't have a cockade, but some volunteers did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have to buy this cockade or was it given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually, one would buy it in Knez Mihajlova Street as a souvenir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the sake of the Chamber, I have to draw your attention to the fact that these two cockades differ from each other, and you should bear that in mind, the one that Razilovic [phoen] has on his chest and the man next to him who is Chetnik, Vojvoda Jovo Ostojic and this witness doesn't know. I kept drawing your attention to the fact that these cockades differ, depending on who manufactured them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, it seems that these two cockades are different. What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite honestly, I didn't pay much attention to the differences among the cockades, between the cockades. I only stated that, yes, he has a cockade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's on the transcript, and the Judges will be very careful with this. Mrs. Biersay, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you mentioned that these items could be bought as souvenirs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there other types of memorabilia or insignia that could be bought as souvenirs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could also buy SCP membership cards in various colours, black with a skull and cross-bones, white, blue. I would take my membership card and go to Zoran Drazilovic and say, "I want my membership card to be different from the others." And I would take that to him and he would put a stamp on it and sign it, and that was a sort of souvenir. Now in Knez Mihajlova, they're selling t-shirts with pictures of Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic. At that time, they were also selling membership cards with different colours, in gold letters, with double-headed eagles, so anyone could choose what they like, whether a separate coat of arms or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the extent that the volunteers in your group seem to have all been monarchists, this cockade that we see, was it a monarchist emblem or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one, now, I really don't know. You can't see it very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did monarchists have a specific symbol or insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it had to have a crown, which signifies the king.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what did you hear the volunteers say about the idea of greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it sounded nice. Everybody liked the idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did the monarchists also like the idea of greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, the monarchists were just helping the people. They weren't thinking along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if I could now direct your attention to the photograph in front of you, which is 4170, and again this comes from the previously-admitted exhibit. Mr. Witness, do you recognise anyone in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only person I recognise on this photograph is Brne. He's one of Seselj's Vojvodas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you mark with an "X", and could we also capture the electronic version as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have difficulty recognising him if he were to take his cap off, but he always wore this cap at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May we have an exhibit number for that photograph and the electronic copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph will become Exhibit P316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you just talked about a Vojvoda. Looking at him, we see that he's in military dress, he's wearing a camouflage uniform with a belt, maybe a weapon, can't really see that, and as you said, he's got this strange headgear. If you remember well, do you remember what the emblem is on this cap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't see very well here. It's all white. I really don't see this very well, but he has these flaps coming down like a sort of curtain from his cap, and he was really distinguishable by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To what unit did he belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite honestly, I knew that he fought in Bosnia, and I know him only by sight. I saw him once in passing, but I don't know the man personally. I heard from others that it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what did the others say about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They said that this was Vojvoda Brne, that Seselj had created him a Vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is a vojvod, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, Seselj can never be a vojvoda because the king has to declare him to be a vojvoda. If Rajic is a vojvoda, he can not create other vojvodas. He's simply turning people's heads, misleading the people. He was making fun of the people, what he did with making these vojvodas, he was making fun of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to you, only a king can create a vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when the king is not reigning, what happens then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then there are no vojvodas either. I can declare myself to be an emperor, Emperor in Majentija [phoen], if there's no king.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we can turn to 65 ter number 4177, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is it that you recognise, and could you indicate by placing an "X"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milika, Ceka, Dacevic, that's him here, and this is Cele.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you put a "1" on the first person you described and a "2" on the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who is the person that you're marking with a "1"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's from Pirvoj [phoen], a Montenegrin. He was also declared to be a vojvoda. Milika, Ceka, Dacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cele another one of the vojvodas declared to be such, and I saw him around in Belgrade. He was a deputy of the radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I move for the admission of this photograph as well as the electronic, annotated version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor knows very well the first and last name of this Chetnik vojvoda and should tell you so. If the witness doesn't know, the Prosecutor does, because this photograph is entering the record. I don't object too it. That's Miroslav Vukovic knows as Cele, a Chetnik vojvoda. The Prosecutor knows this and should tell you so, so that the document in the file is properly marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Cele has a name, Miroslav Vukovic. Are you in agreement with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I agree, but I only know him by his nickname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what does "Cele" mean as a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could now move to 4191, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this photograph, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljubisa Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Can you put a "1" on Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. This is Aleksic and Drazilovic, the one on the far right, Zoran Drazilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you please put a "2" on Aleksic and a "3" on Drazilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And may we have an exhibit number for that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, finally, if we could move to the next photograph, 4221.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Aleksic. I don't know the others, but I saw him several times in passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May we have an exhibit number for this photograph as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just to be clear, Your Honours, the Prosecution is moving for the original photograph as well as the electronically-annotated ones as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want two numbers, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it can be a collection where there are two pages for one exhibit or if it's easier to do it as two numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original is the video, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the video already has a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I believe it's P256. But the photographs have a separate 65 ter number, so I think that's why they're being given separate "P" numbers, exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, because I'm not sure I understand. What is the purpose of having the blank photograph registered as an exhibit as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In my very limited experience, when we get the annotated photographs, they're generally not as clear as the non-annotated ones, so I thought for clarity it would be best just to have both versions, the annotated and unannotated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. So you want the non-annotated photograph with a number, two numbers per photograph, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A and B. Madam Registrar, can you give us the numbers, photograph by photograph, for the non-annotated ones, i.e., the original photo shown on the screen before the witness put in his crosses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It my be time for a break, and we'll resume and you can finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Before giving the floor to Mrs. Biersay, before she finishes, the Trial Chamber may sit tomorrow morning. We planned to sit in the afternoon, but since the Delic chamber is not sitting, we could sit in the morning. Mr. Seselj, as far as you're concerned, is that a problem if we sit in the morning instead of the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that doesn't present a difficulty. I am ready to resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I now give the floor to Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could you tell me how much more time the Prosecutor has so that I know how much time I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Biersay still has 18 minutes. However, Mr. Seselj, if need be, you could start your cross-examination tomorrow, unless you absolutely want to start as of one 1.30, but you will only have 15 minutes then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's quite natural that I wish to know whether I'm going to start today at all so that I can be ready, but I don't mind, 15 minutes today, and then I can continue tomorrow. There's no problem. I'm going to adapt myself to the time remaining and choose the subjects I want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll make it very easy for Mr. Seselj. The Prosecution rests with respect to this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, no questions left. Then we can move on. There is 55 minutes left before a quarter to 2:00, take or leave some minutes, so, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Mr. President, that I'm ready for all surprises thrown on me by the Prosecutor. Nothing can surprise me or take me unawares.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. VS-033, you said that 99 per cent of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were monarchists, were of the monarchist affiliation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now why did they remain volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, the members of the Serbian Radical Party, when on many occasions I spoke against the monarchy in public and not even on the symbols or insignia or the flag of the Serbian Radical Party did we ever have any monarchististic coat of arms or emblems of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm starting out from my own point of view. I was a political illiterate, and most of the volunteers at the beginning of the war were like me, politically illiterate, and some still are to this very day. Now, I haven't become too politically literate in the meantime, but I have learned a few things along the way to read between the lines, and so on when it comes to politics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mean it directly that way, but when people see something is lacking, they have to choose between two evils, the lesser of two evils.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is there anybody normal any political party in Serbia that is monarchist or any party that advocates that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps Vuk Draskovic, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that all the abnormal people have rallied around Vuk Draskovic, is that right, in favour of the monarchy, because to be a monarchist in a state that is a republic would not be normal in the 20th century; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was talking about the monarchy in 1991 about the monarchy. Later on I saw what was going on and that democracy had arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I may. To your knowledge, during the war up until now, were there people who disappeared, Croats and Serbs and Muslims, people who disappeared and that the fate of whom is totally unknown; nobody knows whether they're dead, whether they're abroad? People who really disappeared, were there such people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know the people personally, but I have heard that there were cases like that, of people disappearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, I have to make an objection.
